chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilad, from Umar ibn Yazid, who said:

I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), 'I ask you,' he said, 'Ask.' I said, 'Why did the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) sell the mothers of children?' He said, 'To free their necks [from slavery].' I said, 'And how is that?' He said, 'Any man who bought a slave girl, she bore him a child, and then he did not pay her price and did not leave from his wealth enough to pay it off, her child was taken from her and she was sold, and her price was paid.' I said, 'So they are sold for other than that, from debt?' He said, 'No.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a slave woman who bore her master a child if he cannot pay her price?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq, the specific legal mechanism of 'fakk al-raqabah' (freeing the neck) is clarified as the primary justification for selling an Umm al-Walad to settle her master's unpaid purchase price when he lacks other assets. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential distinction that such sales are strictly tied to debt settlement rather than general financial needs, reinforcing the principle of protecting the maternal bond while ensuring creditor rights. The dialogue underscores the precision of Imami fiqh in distinguishing between specific debt categories and broader financial obligations.
